feedback: If a learner reverses this (says 2/6 > 5/6) by over-applying a 'bigger number means smaller' idea carried over from same-numerator pairs, clarify when each rule applies: 'The bottoms are the same here — sixths are sixths. So just count: is five pieces more or less than two?'
If correct, ask them to read the symbol aloud and confirm it opens toward the larger amount.
activities.intendedInsight: When the denominator is shared, the parts are identical in size, so the fraction with more parts (larger numerator) is larger. This is a DIFFERENT comparison from the same-numerator case and must not be solved by 'bigger bottom = smaller'.
learnerActions: On one whole, shade 5/6 and 2/6 on aligned bars or on a single 0–1 number line.
State that the sixths are all the same size on both.
Decide which is larger by counting how many equal parts are shaded, then write 5/6 __ 2/6.
Explain: 'Same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two, so 5/6 > 2/6.'
activities.title: Same denominator: count the equal parts

feedback: If a learner concludes 3/8 > 3/4 from mismatched drawings, ask: 'Were both bars the same size to begin with? Redraw them the same length and look again.'
If correct, challenge: 'Can you make two fractions where the one with the bigger bottom number is actually the smaller fraction, and show why on equal wholes?'
activities.intendedInsight: When you judge which fraction is larger by looking at shaded regions, both must be drawn on the same whole for the picture to be fair; 3/4 of a small bar can look smaller than 3/8 of a large bar, even though, as numbers, 3/4 > 3/8.
learnerActions: Draw 3/4 on a short bar and 3/8 on a long bar, deliberately mismatched.
Compare the shaded regions by eye and notice the drawing can be misleading.
Redraw both fractions on identical wholes and compare again.
State in your own words why, when you compare by shaded pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole for the comparison to be fair.
activities.title: Does 3/4 always beat 3/8? The same-whole rule

feedback: Accept an answer only when the learner can justify it by part size or count; a right symbol with a digit-only reason ('8 is bigger') should prompt 'bigger what — bigger number, or bigger piece?'
Mix same-numerator and same-denominator items so learners must select the right reasoning each time, not run one rule blindly.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in applying the two lines of reasoning across varied pairs, with the correct rule chosen for the structure of each pair.
learnerActions: Decide the correct sign for same-numerator pairs (e.g. 3/8 vs 3/4) and same-denominator pairs (e.g. 5/6 vs 2/6).
Order short sets of same-numerator fractions and, separately, same-denominator fractions from smallest to largest.
Sort pairs into >, =, and < groups and, where used, match a fraction pair to its symbol.
For each answer, state the reason in part-size/count language rather than quoting digits.
activities.title: Practise and sort comparisons
